HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement
for Harness Token Efficiency

Yuhua Jiang Email: mailto:yh-jiang24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cnblackyh-jiang24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cnmailto:chanx@microsoft.comblackchanx@microsoft.com    Chang Xu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Microsoft Research Asia (MSRA) Email: mailto:feifiegao@tsinghua.edu.cnblackfeifiegao@tsinghua.edu.cnmailto:lizo@microsoft.comblacklizo@microsoft.com    Feifei Gao    Li Zhao Affiliation: Tsinghua University Microsoft Research Asia (MSRA)
Abstract

Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model–tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43% to 85.71% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.

1 Introduction

Agent harnesses connect model reasoning to tool execution. ReAct alternates reasoning, actions and observations [46]; SWE-agent demonstrates that interface design shapes software-engineering performance [44], and Toolformer learns when to call APIs [33]. After each tool result, the harness must decide whether the observation demands new reasoning or merely permits an already resolved action to execute. Repeated deliberation can regenerate decisions whose semantics have not changed.

Efficiency methods intervene at different points. Prompt compression and history management reduce the input replayed into a call [16, 17, 30, 42, 21]. Fast–slow architectures and routing change who reasons and how deeply [4, 45, 27]. Executable skills, observation-independent plans and compiled tool dependencies reuse or schedule prior computation [40, 43, 19]. ActionEngine further executes task programs against reusable application memory with reactive repair [52]. These methods already establish the value of programmatic execution. HarnessMM studies a narrower contract: an episode-specific action remains literal, later feedback changes its eligibility, and the execution record identifies the reasoning boundary actually bypassed.

Feedback can optimize instructions and agent programs through APE, STOP, ADAS, Self-Refine and Reflexion [53, 49, 13, 24, 36]. Such optimization constructs a harness; its deployment still determines which callbacks recur. Jev’s typed probability interface [1] motivates compact candidate selection, but adding a selector does not remove the original callback automatically. We call this accounting mismatch the Substitution Paradox: computation is saved only when eliminated reasoning exceeds added authorship, selection and recovery.

A concrete opportunity appears when slow reasoning fixes several actions before their execution feedback arrives. After writing a program, the next compilation command can already be specified; after compilation, a successful return code can activate an already-specified test command. We call a decision resolved when prior reasoning has fixed its action and literal arguments; the unknown tool receipt determines whether that action is ready to execute. The example separates semantic uncertainty from execution uncertainty and suggests a different role for feedback: activating a resolved decision. Our insight is that such decisions can persist across feedback boundaries as guarded executable commitments. An authored graph can serve multiple transitions while its continuations remain resolved; new inference returns control to the slow actor, which may reason and author further graphs throughout the task.

We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency by changing when the harness invokes its reasoning model (Figure 1). HarnessMM inserts a controller at the native decision boundary while keeping model weights, tools and task interfaces fixed. Executable Decision Graphs (EDGs) store actions and literal arguments already resolved by slow reasoning, together with their dependencies and public execution guards. Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR) retains these decisions across tool transitions and checks whether observed receipts satisfy their guards. Certified Callback Substitution (CCS) then dispatches the stored action through the native interface and omits the corresponding reasoning callback. A typed selector chooses an eligible decision or abstains; new semantic decisions, unsupported evidence and abstention return control to the original actor. This changes the harness’s execution policy so that resolved actions avoid repeated context input and reasoning output while unresolved decisions retain access to the original reasoning process. Complete-task accounting includes graph authorship, selection, remaining slow calls, fallback and unsuccessful executions. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) iteratively refines companion harness configurations: the current harness supplies training feedback for candidate edits, validation selects the retained candidate, and that harness supplies the next round’s training feedback. The selected configuration is frozen before test evaluation (Appendix B.2).

We integrate HarnessMM into Codex and DeepSeek Harness and evaluate each against its original harness. On the same 98 HumanEval test tasks, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02, a 29.54% saving. For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43% to 85.71% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62, an 87.93% saving (Section 5.3). These comparisons demonstrate that improving when a harness invokes reasoning and executes actions can reduce token consumption while preserving or improving task performance. An MBPP ablation isolates persistent decision reuse and callback removal, measuring 26.91% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52% lower cost than retained callbacks. Companion studies evaluate their benchmark-specific instruction and context configurations separately (Section 5.4).

Our contributions are:

  • •

    EDGs separate resolved action semantics from feedback-dependent readiness, making prior deliberation executable at future tool boundaries.

  • •

    GDR retains the graph and uses public receipts to activate causally ordered actions while reserving new decisions for slow reasoning.

  • •

    CCS substitutes native execution for registered callbacks and verifies omission with receipt-bound certificates. The MBPP ablation measures how reuse and callback substitution affect success and complete task cost.

2 Related Work

Prompt, context and reasoning compression.

LLMLingua and its successors compress prompt inputs [16, 17, 30]; AgentDiet and observation masking reduce replayed trajectory context [42, 21]. Thinking budgets control generated reasoning [15]. These methods reduce the size or depth of a call; HarnessMM targets whether that call needs to recur at all.

Fast–slow agents and model routing.

Talker–Reasoner separates response and planning [4]; CogRouter adapts cognitive depth [45]; boundary-guided routing chooses the reasoning model [50]. Jev motivates typed compact decisions [1]. Our Jev-motivated typed selector uses a candidate-ID/abstention interface, with single-token decoding when selection requires a model call. HarnessMM studies whether such a compact decision actually removes a future reasoning callback.

Skills, memory and reusable programs.

Chain-of-thought prompting exposes intermediate reasoning [41], Voyager retains executable skills [40], and SkillLens retrieves procedural context [25]. A skill or macro can inform future reasoning or encapsulate a routine. An EDG instead stores episode-specific, fully resolved semantic commitments; public execution conditions control their activation. This distinction allows execution to replace a reasoning call rather than merely guide it.

Agent and harness optimization.

APE, STOP and ADAS improve prompts, programs and agent configurations from feedback [53, 49, 13]. Self-modification methods extend the search to improvement operators [47, 51, 38]. HarnessMM changes when a harness calls its reasoning model and when it directly executes a previously resolved action. Instruction optimization, context compaction and RSI supply companion configurations; they are outside the core execution method and retain separate experimental attribution. Their development protocols and costs appear in Appendix B.2.

3 Problem Formulation

3.1 Reasoning calls and tool actions in a harness

The actor parameters θ\theta are fixed. An existing harness hh supplies instructions, context and native execution rules. HarnessMM intervenes at its reasoning callbacks: a stored action may replace a new model call. For task xx, unroll a finite execution under the benchmark limits into a computation graph 𝒢h​(x)=(V,E)\mathcal{G}_{h}(x)=(V,E). Nodes include reasoning, retrieval, routing, tools, verification and recovery; edges encode execution dependencies. For policy π\pi, node vv has model-token cost cvc_{v}, giving

C⁡(π)=𝔼⁡[∑v∈V𝟏​{v​ invoked under ​π}​cv].C(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{v\in V}\mathbf{1}\{v\text{ invoked under }\pi\}\,c_{v}\right]. (1)

The fast–slow policy changes which reasoning nodes recur after public feedback. Deterministic tools use no actor tokens but affect subsequent calls and quality. Both node costs and invocation probabilities can change when a continuation is substituted. We use sts_{t} for public state at transition tt: the request, observed tool feedback and completed action history.

3.2 Capability-constrained computation substitution

Let Qb​(h)=𝔼⁡[mb​(Runθ⁡(x;h))]Q_{b}(h)=\mathbb{E}[m_{b}(\operatorname{Run}_{\theta}(x;h))], where mbm_{b} is benchmark bb’s official score. Relative to the original harness h0h_{0}, define capability regret Rb​(π)=Qb​(h0)−Qb​(hπ)R_{b}(\pi)=Q_{b}(h_{0})-Q_{b}(h_{\pi}). The objective is

minπ⁡C⁡(π)subject toRb​(π)≤ϵb\min_{\pi}C(\pi)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R_{b}(\pi)\leq\epsilon_{b} (2)

for every declared quality endpoint, equivalently Qb​(hπ)≥Qb​(h0)−ϵbQ_{b}(h_{\pi})\geq Q_{b}(h_{0})-\epsilon_{b}. This is a policy-level constraint, assessed by evaluating both harnesses on the same tasks. Tolerances are fixed before evaluation; zero-regret protocols use ϵb=0\epsilon_{b}=0. Both harnesses are evaluated on the full task set to assess the constraint, including unsuccessful tasks. The original tools, evaluator and limits are shared within each comparison. Finite-sample score differences and uncertainty are reported under the bound protocol (Appendix B.2).

3.3 The Substitution Paradox

The paradox arises when fast–slow composition adds a decision without removing its downstream deliberation. If a fast stage costs CfC_{f} but removes none of an original continuation’s CnC_{n} tokens, its additive path costs Cn+CfC_{n}+C_{f}. Short output alone cannot resolve this overhead: typed output and frequent fast-path activation do not establish callback elimination. A beneficial substitution requires

Cremoved>Cintroduced,C_{\mathrm{removed}}>C_{\mathrm{introduced}}, (3)

where introduced computation includes authorship, routing, additional context and any fallback or recovery. This cost condition and the capability constraint address separate requirements.

4 HarnessMM: Reusing Decisions

HarnessMM changes the route from tool feedback to the next native action. EDG stores resolved decisions, GDR determines their eligibility, and CCS substitutes native execution for registered slow callbacks. The controller integrates with an existing harness through its public-state adapter, slow-call entry point and native action dispatcher.

Method boundary and fixed configuration.

The core method decides whether a stored action can replace the next reasoning call. Prompt editing, context compaction and finalization rules configure the surrounding harness. They are developed on training data, selected before evaluation and held fixed during each run. The runtime selector chooses an eligible EDG node or abstains; it does not choose which optimization techniques to combine. Appendix D.5 maps each reported configuration to its actual intervention.

Figure 1 separates harness RSI from execution within a task. The upper row shows RSI revising the harness using training task results and complete token cost; the lower row shows the GDR and CCS graph edits. At runtime, the controller ingests each public receipt, updates eligibility, and either executes a stored action or invokes the slow actor. The latter can resolve new decisions and author another graph.

4.1 Executable Decision Graphs (EDG)

An EDG stores actions whose semantics and arguments slow reasoning has already resolved. For example, a coding actor can fix a file-write action, a make command and a pytest command. Public guards determine whether these stored actions can execute; later receipts supply readiness evidence without regenerating their arguments.

At slow decision ii, actor H0H_{0} emits the current tool action and an EDG Gi=(Vi,Ei)G_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}), a bounded executable continuation. Its future decision nodes are

Bi={d1,…,dm},dj=(aj,argj,predj,gj).B_{i}=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{m}\},\qquad d_{j}=(a_{j},\mathrm{arg}_{j},\mathrm{pred}_{j},g_{j}). (4)

Here aja_{j} is the native action, argj\mathrm{arg}_{j} its complete literal arguments, predj\mathrm{pred}_{j} its predecessor and gj:𝒮public→{true,false}g_{j}:\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{public}}\rightarrow\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\} its public execution guard. The author fixes gjg_{j} with the node; the adapter evaluates it against subsequently observed receipts. Each node has its own guard.

The input EDG in Figure 1 combines reasoning, context compaction, fast decisions and tool use. For the coding example, guards can check a missing file, available build inputs or a successful build. Dependencies must also be complete. Edges connect the root or an earlier node to a successor, forming an acyclic graph. Missing or rejecting receipts prevent admission; an empty graph returns control to the slow actor.

4.2 Guarded Decision Reuse (GDR)

GDR retains the graph across tool transitions. The green GDR panel shows how a condition guard enables a reuse route around repeated reasoning. Each observed receipt updates predecessor completion and guard truth. Eligibility requires closed arguments needing no new semantic inference. For node djd_{j},

eligible⁡(dj,st)=𝟏​{predj​ completed}⋅𝟏{gj(st)=true}⋅𝟏{argj closed}.\begin{split}\operatorname{eligible}(d_{j},s_{t})={}&\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{pred}_{j}\text{ completed}\}\\ &\cdot\mathbf{1}\{g_{j}(s_{t})=\mathrm{true}\}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{arg}_{j}\text{ closed}\}.\end{split} (5)

The eligible set is ℰ⁡(st)={dj∈Bi:eligible⁡(dj,st)=1}\mathcal{E}(s_{t})=\{d_{j}\in B_{i}:\operatorname{eligible}(d_{j},s_{t})=1\}. Guards consume observed receipts, never predicted results. Unsupported observations, unmet dependencies or arguments requiring new inference defer to H0H_{0}.

Implementation banks serialize the nodes and edges (Appendix C.4). Literal closure is enforced by the schema and candidate-membership checks; whether prior reasoning correctly resolved an action remains a semantic assumption assessed through task scoring. A passing guard proves its declared public condition, rather than general task correctness.

A Jev-motivated typed selector returns an eligible candidate ID or abstains, without revising arguments. A unique eligible node can execute deterministically. Empty sets and abstention invoke the slow actor. Each execution receipt updates the same graph. Appendix C specifies the public-state adapter and native integration.

4.3 Certified Callback Substitution (CCS)

CCS converts an admitted GDR decision into an executable replacement for the next slow callback. It runs the exact authored action through the original tool interface and binds the resulting receipt to the omitted callback. At a registered original execution boundary, the parent follows st→H0→ats_{t}\!\to\!H_{0}\!\to\!a_{t}. An admitted EDG decision instead follows st→dj→ats_{t}\!\to\!d_{j}\!\to\!a_{t} through the same original tool interface. A substitution certificate binds

κt=(CLOSEgraph​_​hash,decision​_​id,predecessor​_​receipt,OPENexact​_​args,tool​_​receipt,bypassed​_​callback​_​id).\begin{split}\kappa_{t}=(&\mathrm{graph\_hash},\mathrm{decision\_id},\mathrm{predecessor\_receipt},\\ &\mathrm{exact\_args},\mathrm{tool\_receipt},\mathrm{bypassed\_callback\_id}).\end{split} (6)

The fingerprint graph​_​hash\mathrm{graph\_hash} identifies the authored graph content, and decision​_​id\mathrm{decision\_id} identifies its node. The remaining fields bind the predecessor’s completion, exact executed arguments, actual tool result and omitted callback. The orange CCS panel depicts this substitution: a certified callback replaces the redundant reasoning subgraph and retains its execution dependencies.

The audit matches this fingerprint and decision ID to literal arguments, the completed predecessor’s callback and receipt, and the tool execution receipt. It checks the registered parent boundary and requires

Nslow,tparent−Nslow,tHarnessMM≥1.N^{\mathrm{parent}}_{\mathrm{slow},t}-N^{\mathrm{HarnessMM}}_{\mathrm{slow},t}\geq 1. (7)

The parent count registers the original callback boundary. The certificate verifies exact native execution and absence of that request, without predicting its unobserved response or token count. Native scoring measures task correctness; complete-task totals measure cost. Appendix F.3 records the receipt audit.

4.4 Complete-Task Accounting

The optimization target is complete episode cost:

Cepisode​(h,x)=∑c∈𝒞⁡(h,x)(Tcin+Tcout).C_{\mathrm{episode}}(h;x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}(h,x)}(T_{c}^{\mathrm{in}}+T_{c}^{\mathrm{out}}). (8)

The ledger charges authorship, selector inputs and outputs, added context, remaining slow calls, fallback, recovery, finalization and failed paid executions. Cached input remains counted. Deterministic checks add CPU work and no actor tokens. Historical and MiMo Codex displays retain their declared scope; complete-cost benefit claims require all physical requests.

Development cost CdevC_{\mathrm{dev}} is reported separately, including training, proposals, protected validation and rejected attempts. For NN deployment tasks,

C¯N=CdevN+𝔼x​[Cepisode​(h,x)].\overline{C}_{N}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{dev}}}{N}+\mathbb{E}_{x}[C_{\mathrm{episode}}(h;x)]. (9)

Shared authoring is charged exactly once to its declared development or execution cohort. This deployment amortization is separate from reuse within an episode. Token cost does not establish latency or energy savings; those require separate measurements.

Selecting the surrounding configuration.

Training develops author prompts, context settings and adapter rules. Disjoint validation selects among training-frozen configurations; the selected implementation is frozen before testing. These offline choices set the inputs and action contract of the execution controller. They remain distinct from its online choice between an eligible stored action and slow reasoning. Appendix B.2 gives the development protocols. Appendix D specifies the execution algorithm, assumptions and structural invariants.

5 Experiments

5.1 Evaluation protocol

All methods use the same tasks, backbone, original tools, task limits and scorer. All compared methods, including baselines and native harnesses, receive token-efficiency prompts and an explicit objective to reduce complete-task input-plus-output token consumption while preserving task performance. Success uses the benchmark evaluation endpoint, and token cost includes input plus output for all paid calls, including failures. Development optimization cost is reported separately from complete-task execution. Full-population coding comparisons use custom 20/20/60 splits: HumanEval 33/33/98 and MBPP 85/85/257, with deterministic rounding and fixed task IDs. TRAIN supplies revisions, validation selects TRAIN-frozen candidates, and TEST measures the selected configuration. The coding ablations evaluate the core execution method; native harness pairs evaluate its integration with fixed context and finalization settings. Figure 2 retains the companion studies. Appendix D.5 identifies their differing mechanisms, populations and cost scope.

5.2 Does fast execution substitute slow reasoning?

Table 1 reports model-call and substitution statistics on 98 HumanEval and 257 MBPP-sanitized test tasks. On HumanEval, the DeepSeek Harness falls from 954 to 415 paid model calls, with 147 certified callback bypasses (1.50/task); Codex falls from 524 to 499 calls, with 18 certified bypasses (0.18/task). On MBPP-sanitized, DeepSeek Harness falls from 1,633 to 1,088 calls, with 472 certified bypasses (1.84/task), while success rises from 90.27% to 91.83%. The MBPP-sanitized Codex pair records 91.83% and 90.66% success at 129.55 and 49.22 Tokens/task (k) (Appendix L.1). The original harnesses have zero certified bypasses. All rates use the full task set for each method.

The second ablation in Section 5.5 isolates persistent GDR reuse and CCS callback substitution with the same execution settings.

5.3 Industrial harness results

We use the official Codex and DeepSeek Harness runtimes [28, 5], with the same pinned backbone, original interface and scorer within each pair. HumanEval supplies a complete held-out comparison: Codex preserves 90.82% success with 66.72 versus 47.02 Tokens/task (k) (29.54% saving); DeepSeek Harness improves from 71.43% to 85.71% with 96.28 versus 11.62 Tokens/task (k) (87.93% saving). Paired outcomes show five improvements and five regressions for Codex; DeepSeek Harness has 22 improvements and eight regressions (two-sided exact McNemar p=0.0161p=0.0161). These integrated harness effects combine literal-bank reuse, context management and finalization. Their total call-count difference is therefore not an isolated effect of certificates; the MBPP ablations below isolate persistence and callback retention. The MiMo-v2.6-pro DeepSeek Harness comparison completes the same 98-task population: baseline success is 96.94% and HarnessMM success is 97.96%, with 11.62 versus 4.40 Tokens/task (k) (62.12% saving). Figure 3(e) reports this MiMo pair separately from the Qwen comparisons; the MiMo Codex pair completes the same 98-task evaluation at 93.88% versus 94.90% success. Its costs are 62.60 versus 10.09 Tokens/task (k); MiMo MBPP Codex completes the same 257-task evaluation at 96.50% versus 97.28% success, with 47.56 versus 11.00 Tokens/task (k); the MiMo DeepSeek Harness pair completes the same 257-task population at 97.67% versus 98.05% success, with 6.20 versus 5.11 Tokens/task (k). Slow reasoning authors literal action banks, and CPU receipt guards execute 480 native substitutions (Appendix L.1).

On MBPP, the complete Qwen-backed DeepSeek Harness comparison improves from 90.27% to 91.83%, while Tokens/task (k) fall from 53.98 to 10.61 (80.35% saving). Slow reasoning authors executable action banks; fast guarded execution performs 472 certified substitutions. The CoT-only baseline reaches 93.39% at 15.04 Tokens/task (k), giving a 29.46% HarnessMM saving. Figure 3(c) reports this held-out pair; the independent Codex comparison records 91.83% and 90.66% success, at 129.55 and 49.22 Tokens/task (k).

Historical MBPP and GAIA2 development comparisons remain in Figure 3 and Appendix D; they retain their development scope.

5.4 Companion configurations: quality and cost

Figure 2 presents ALFWorld, SearchQA, LiveMath, AIME, Terminal-Bench 2 and GAIA2 in their original order, with No Skill, SkillOpt, AutoSaddler and HarnessMM in each panel. The HarnessMM label identifies each study’s selected configuration. ALFWorld varies instructions; SearchQA uses input routing, a compact-rule draft and paid fallback; LiveMath changes the answer-first prompt and output cap; AIME uses a compiled decision policy with domain fallback; the archived Terminal panel uses an instruction policy. GAIA2 combines a literal bank with context handling. These companion studies measure their stated configurations. The MBPP ablation supplies the direct test of EDG persistence and callback removal (Appendix D.5).

On complete SearchQA validation, HarnessMM reaches 76.76% EM at 0.99 Tokens/task (k), saving 19.08% against No Skill (paired 95% interval [16.57,21.23][16.57,21.23]%), 38.57% against SkillOpt and 20.75% against AutoSaddler (Table 21). On all 560 AIME test questions, HarnessMM reaches 87.14% accuracy, compared with 86.96% for No Skill, 87.86% for SkillOpt and 88.04% for AutoSaddler. HarnessMM uses 5.90 Tokens/task (k), including shared authorship: 14.94% below SkillOpt, 28.34% above No Skill and 20.44% above AutoSaddler. The cost decomposition in Table 15 shows 0.54 input, 4.28 output and 1.08 shared-author Tokens/task (k). No Skill uses 0.22 input and 4.38 output Tokens/task (k): generated reasoning dominates this mathematical workload. The small reduction in HarnessMM’s execution output is outweighed by its additional input and authorship. The comparison uses one execution per question under the same frozen model and native scoring protocol. SkillOpt uses three completed training rounds; AutoSaddler retains its completed four-round policy. The separate original 18-question AIME 2025 comparison remains in Appendix I.1. On all 480 GAIA2 test scenarios, HarnessMM reaches 43.96% success with 639.64 Tokens/task (k), compared with 42.71% and 730.22 for No Skill, 46.88% and 770.63 for SkillOpt, and 42.08% and 772.22 for AutoSaddler. HarnessMM reduces complete actor cost by 12.41%, 17.00% and 17.17%, respectively. The integrated harness performs 146 verified fast native executions (1.40% of all action attempts); input accounts for 99.47% of its actor cost (Table 16). It gains 1.25 percentage points over No Skill while remaining 2.92 points below SkillOpt. Each scenario runs once per method after frozen validation selection; all unsuccessful executions remain in the quality and cost aggregates. Appendix I reports a separate quality–cost study of development candidates and frozen GAIA2 validation results.

Under the common ALFWorld actor, HarnessMM’s frozen instructions achieve the highest observed success and lowest model-token cost among the four instruction policies: 66.20% at 31.12 Tokens/task (k). SkillOpt reaches 63.29% at 101.33 Tokens/task (k). The paired success difference is 2.91 points (95% floorplan-cluster interval [0.43,5.61][0.43,5.61]), with 69.29% fewer model tokens. Table 8 reports the four freshly executed instruction-only conditions. The complete benchmark replay and accounting are documented in Appendix G.1.

ALFWorld task-family instruction ablation.

Figure 4 compares six frozen instruction conditions on the same 2,133 tasks across seeds 9401, 9402 and 9403. HarnessMM averages 65.70% success at 31.44 Tokens/task (k). The task-family paragraph alone reaches 62.01% at 28.69 Tokens/task (k); general guidance alone reaches 49.21% at 38.94 Tokens/task (k). The family-only condition is cheaper but loses 3.69 success points. Its per-seed paired 95% floorplan-cluster intervals are [2.61,6.21][2.61,6.21], [0.48,3.76][0.48,3.76] and [2.68,6.48][2.68,6.48].

The remaining instruction conditions and per-seed paired intervals appear in Appendix I.3. All use the common actor and 50-step limit. These ablations isolate instruction content, rather than EDG execution.

5.5 GDR and CCS ablation on MBPP

Our second ablation isolates GDR and CCS on MBPP-sanitized [2] with DeepSeek Harness and a fixed backbone. Figure 4 compares four conditions on the same 257 tasks. Full HarnessMM reaches 93.77% success at 13.17 Tokens/task (k), versus 93.00% and 18.03 for W/o GDR (single-use EDG). GDR reduces complete cost by 26.91%, with a task-paired adjusted interval of [4.01, 45.57]%.

Full HarnessMM makes 407 certified substitutions, including repeated bypasses in 201 graphs. W/o CCS (callbacks retained) reaches 93.39% at 16.37 Tokens/task (k), a measured 19.52% cost reduction for full HarnessMM. Disabling EDG execution reaches 95.33% at 16.19: full HarnessMM uses 18.62% fewer tokens but solves four fewer tasks. Certificates verify removal; their independent benefit is not ablated. Appendix E gives the shared execution settings, paired uncertainty and historical comparison.

Evidence attribution.

The complete coding comparisons measure integrated harness quality and cost. The single-use and retained-callback ablations directly test persistent reuse and callback removal. Instruction-only ALFWorld measures instruction content. Certificates establish execution and omission, while native scoring establishes quality; no per-certificate token value is assumed.

5.6 HarnessMM harness RSI

Figure 5 shows eight training-guided harness RSI iterations on the same 32 MiniWoB++ training tasks. Each pair shares the actor, author prompt, full screenshots, coordinate compiler, guards, fallback, native scorer and limits; single-use EDGs permit one future execution per graph, while HarnessMM retains eligible decisions. Training feedback refines visual grounding and screenshot context. Disjoint validation selects a frozen configuration before testing.

Across the first eight iterations, HarnessMM success rises from 34.38% to 90.63%, while Tokens/task (k) fall from 3.26 to 1.06 (67.43%). At the eighth iteration, both arms solve 29 of 32 tasks; persistence saves 29.83% (1.51 versus 1.06 Tokens/task (k); paired task-bootstrap 95% interval [18.84,39.00]%[18.84,39.00]\%). Calls/task fall from 1.47 to 1.03, with 16 second-and-later executions within retained graphs.

These are complete episode execution costs. Appendix A gives the measurements and their separate development-cost scope.

6 Limitations

Savings depend on provider input, cache and context accounting and on the availability of resolved actions. New semantic decisions require slow reasoning. Authorship, selection and recovery can outweigh avoided calls. Public-state adapters are task specific, and small development sets leave policy-level quality differences uncertain.

7 Conclusion

HarnessMM improves harness token efficiency by storing resolved decisions, checking when they can execute and using them to replace repeated reasoning calls. Complete HumanEval comparisons on all 98 test tasks preserve Codex success at 90.82% with 29.54% fewer actor tokens and improve DeepSeek Harness from 71.43% to 85.71% with 87.93% fewer tokens. The MBPP ablation isolates persistence and callback removal; companion studies retain their own configuration scope.

Appendix A HarnessMM visual harness RSI study

The eight MiniWoB++ harness RSI iterations in Figure 5 evaluate HarnessMM. Every RSI iteration evaluates all 32 training tasks once per arm, with identical task instances and actor seed. The actor is Qwen3.5-9B; inputs are full screenshots, the action limit is 15 and the episode allowance is 180 seconds. Single-use EDG permits one future execution per authored graph. HarnessMM retains eligible nodes across later tool-feedback boundaries. Both arms share the iteration-specific author prompt, public screenshot context, coordinate compiler, visual guards and fallback. These shared components develop across chronological RSI iterations. The curve measures training-guided harness RSI; it is not a series of autonomous optimizer rounds or held-out test evaluations.

Tokens/task (k) equals complete actor input-plus-output tokens divided by 32 and 1,000. Calls/task counts every measured physical model request, including authorship, native reasoning, retained callbacks and paid fallbacks, divided by all 32 tasks. Every episode’s authorship, native reasoning, control, fallback and unsuccessful requests is charged. Optimization, candidate selection, validation and historical research costs are outside these per-iteration execution measurements and remain in the separate complete ledgers. Accordingly, the curve measures candidate execution efficiency. The paired interval at the eighth RSI iteration resamples tasks within the same fixed task set; there is one execution per task and arm.

Appendix B Implementation and selection

B.1 QA profiles and execution

At round kk, the QA harness stores profiles hD,kh_{\mathrm{D},k} (DELETE) and hM,kh_{\mathrm{M},k} (MODIFY). Initially, MODIFY adds five answer-normalization rules to DELETE; the remaining four sections and answer contract are identical. A frozen linear head selects MODIFY when g⁡(x)≥κg(x)\geq\kappa, and DELETE otherwise. Its eight input-only features are context token count, document count, question character and token counts, question–context lexical coverage, quoted-span and relation-cue indicators, and named-token count. The archived threshold maximizes discovery exact matches using five-fold out-of-fold predictions, subject to at least 8% token saving and at most 5% harm relative to SkillOpt. Deployment reads frozen hD,Kh_{\mathrm{D},K} and hM,Kh_{\mathrm{M},K} without a router-model call, generated answers or reference labels. Interactive tasks instead use their task-family instructions.

The full-source QA adapter retrieves original rule sentences from the selected profile, retaining normalization and answer-format rules. It supplies these sentences and the complete context to a draft call with a 512-token output cap. Format, source-location and explicit answer-type checks either accept the draft unchanged or restore the complete selected profile in a second actor call. Explicit negative/comparison questions and multiple blanks bypass the draft. All draft and fallback tokens are charged. Earlier compact-context and model-selected variants have separate identities (Appendix J).

B.2 Recorded rule-development protocol

The historical textual pilot uses the original routed QA adapter and 32/32/32/128 source-group-disjoint tasks for training, inner validation, meta validation and the final screen. This four-role protocol predates the custom 20/20/60 comparisons. Training feedback contains responses, official scores, token usage and successful cases to preserve. A fixed compiler applies proposed edits to named rule slots after checking the parent hash, schema, permitted fields and size constraints. It rejects executable code, answer literals and case-specific facts. Retained rules and answer contracts keep their source bytes; invalid proposals alias the parent and remain charged.

A child passes the harness gate only if it changes the harness, preserves the parent’s EM and F1 on both validation splits, uses at most 90% of Original’s inference tokens on both, and improves at least one quality or cost endpoint over the parent. Fixed-policy RSI ranks passing children by meta-validation EM, then F1, then lower cost. Rejection retains the parent; the next round obtains fresh training feedback from the retained harness. Actor weights, routing, execution code, task interfaces, scorers and output caps stay fixed.

The restricted MetaRSI branch [38] also proposes a strategy π~k\widetilde{\pi}_{k} from training feedback. Old and new strategies receive the same parent and feedback and produce separate children. Joint acceptance requires a changed strategy and a distinct child that passes the harness gate, matches or exceeds the old-strategy child’s EM and F1 at no greater cost on each validation split, and improves at least one endpoint strictly on meta validation. Rejection retains (hk,πk)(h_{k},\pi_{k}), including any previously accepted strategy change; ordinary RSI keeps πk=π0\pi_{k}=\pi_{0}. Protected validation examples and answers never enter proposal prompts. Frozen final releases must improve EM and F1 over both Original and fixed-policy RSI, save at least 10% of Original’s inference tokens, and use no more tokens than fixed-policy RSI. These final-screen requirements are separate from round acceptance.

Both branches run two rounds with two child opportunities per round and perform no harness RSI; MetaRSI also accepts no strategy update. Six of eight proposals fail the literal-overlap guard; the two valid three-rule edits add 0.06 and 0.06 input Tokens/task (k) on the 32 inner-validation tasks without improving quality or output usage. Original, fixed-policy RSI, restricted MetaRSI and Original A/A consequently retain identical final request bytes: each solves 78.91% of tasks (78.91 EM, 86.59 F1) using 3.02 Tokens/task (k). Detailed acquisition costs are retained in the external reproduction records. Unchanged deployment cost gives no finite token break-even. The complete eight-arm screen and stage ledger remain in generated/meta_pilot_appendix.tex and generated/meta_optimization_costs.tex.

Appendix C Executable continuation implementation and historical adapters

GDR reuses the authored graph across tool transitions, while CCS executes admitted actions in place of slow callbacks and certifies their removal. The EDG notation names the executable conditional graph represented by the coding adapter’s serialized action bank. Bank hashes identify the serialized graph in the archived audit. The native adapter checks predecessor completion, literal arguments and observed public guards before executing a node. Receipt errors, nonzero return codes, missing dependencies and unknown or false guards return control to slow reasoning. A unique eligible node takes a deterministic path with zero selector tokens. Frozen adapter settings and source identities remain in the external reproduction artifacts. The complete actor ledger includes authorship, selection, fallback and recovery.

The complete MBPP training set (85 tasks) SDK comparison records 153 certified substitutions and 62 public-guard confirmations, with all physical actor costs reconciled. Its policy is the historical structured literal-bank v23 candidate. The complete selected MBPP test set (257 tasks) comparison in Appendix L evaluates the separately frozen v66 candidate. The Codex compound-bank v10 candidate records three certified substitutions but does not pass the broader adoption gate. The training attribution audit appears in Appendix F.3. The historical companion-policy vocabulary includes DELETE, BYPASS, SUBSTITUTE, COMPACT, CACHE/REUSE, TERMINATE and COLLAPSE. It describes the surrounding configuration search, rather than additional modules of the EDG/GDR/CCS execution method. Recovery and finalization rules retain their declared per-run settings.

C.1 Execution variability and paired instruction effects

For task tt, let xtx_{t} be its fixed input: the task request, supplied context, and, for a visual task, an image vtv_{t}. Running the same task more than once need not produce the same answer. We write the rr-th complete execution as yt,r=Runθ⁡(xt,h,zt,r)y_{t,r}=\operatorname{Run}_{\theta}(x_{t};h,z_{t,r}), where Runθ\operatorname{Run}_{\theta} combines slow actor calls, fast selection and tool execution operators. The input xtx_{t}, harness hh, and actor parameters θ\theta are fixed across repeats; zt,rz_{t,r} captures execution conditions such as scheduling, co-batched requests, cache state, and implementation-level variation. A client can prescribe a concurrency and submission schedule ss, but cannot thereby fix the server’s microbatch or numerical path. Below, ii indexes decisions within one execution, and kk indexes offline rule-development rounds.

To measure an instruction edit, we compare the original and edited harnesses under the same prescribed schedule. Let mbm_{b} be benchmark bb’s official metric for an answer or episode, and let yt​(h,s)y_{t}(h,s) denote the response under harness hh and schedule ss. The expected score change from replacing hh with h′h^{\prime} is

τt​(h′,h,s)=𝔼⁡[mb​(yt​(h′,s))−mb​(yt​(h,s))].\tau_{t}(h^{\prime},h;s)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[m_{b}(y_{t}(h^{\prime},s))-m_{b}(y_{t}(h,s))\right]. (10)

The expectation averages over execution conditions within that schedule. Repeated paired executions help separate the edit’s effect from run-to-run variation; one correct-to-wrong transition cannot do so. We report each benchmark and quality endpoint separately.

C.2 Inputs, outputs, and integration

HarnessMM wraps an existing decision procedure H0H_{0} and preserves its original input and output contracts. The developer supplies a task adapter; deployment then accepts the same task request xx as the original agent. The adapter builds public state sis_{i} from the supplied context, current observation, and completed interaction history. It exposes candidate decisions 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i} and a predicate ci​(d)c_{i}(d) specifying which candidates have local support.

A decision has a type and a payload. We write an action decision as Act⁡(a)\operatorname{Act}(a): it executes a tool command and, if the task continues, receives feedback for the next decision. A terminal decision Finish⁡(y)\operatorname{Finish}(y) returns an answer and ends the task. Fixed-context QA is the terminal-decision case of this interface. The adapter defines the domain semantics, while the shared controller owns support admission, candidate membership checks, commitment, and actor fallback.

The original actor parameters, original tools, and evaluator remain fixed. The integration requires a public-state adapter and does not assume that arbitrary task semantics can be inferred automatically.

The offline RSI loop follows a fixed proposal strategy. The current harness runs on training tasks; their execution feedback guides candidate instruction edits. Disjoint validation tasks determine which candidate to retain, and the retained harness supplies the next round’s training feedback. The selected configuration is frozen before final evaluation and deployment. Appendix B records the development protocols.

C.3 Shared commit-or-defer control

At each decision, the adapter prepares a candidate d^i\widehat{d}_{i} and its public support record. The controller applies

di={d^i,d^i∈𝒟i,ci(d^i)=1,H0​(x,Ii,si),otherwise.d_{i}=\begin{cases}\widehat{d}_{i},&\widehat{d}_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{i},\ c_{i}(\widehat{d}_{i})=1,\\ H_{0}(x,I_{i},s_{i}),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (11)

Here IiI_{i} is the instruction text supplied to the original actor. An empty candidate set, unsupported state, or rejected candidate takes the actor path. Both routes return the same typed decision to the original interface, which commits it once. Nonterminal action feedback updates si+1s_{i+1}; a terminal answer ends execution without another state update.

Candidate production and support checks have separate roles. An action adapter can propose a tool command without calling a model; a QA adapter first pays for an actor-generated draft. The controller records the selected route and rejection reason, and the cost ledger includes all model calls made by either adapter. The benchmark scorer evaluates the selected decisions.

For action tasks, the initial actor call supplies the first transition. Local execution then applies at every supported state. An explicit QA bypass supplies no candidate and skips draft generation, so the controller invokes the original answering procedure directly.

C.4 Action adapter: CoT-authored conditional execution

The coding adapter separates constructing an action from deciding whether the current feedback permits it. In a slow turn, the original CoT actor [41] emits a terminal command and a bounded action bank, the serialized EDG. Each bank entry is b=(ℓ,p,g,a)b=(\ell,p,g,a): a label ℓ\ell, a predecessor pp, a condition gg on public tool results, and literal tool arguments aa. A predecessor is the current root command or an earlier entry, so the bank defines an acyclic execution graph. The actor declares future commands only when their arguments are already determined; unseen data requires a new slow turn.

After a command returns, the adapter exposes entries whose predecessor was that command. The fast selector receives the original user request, original tool schema, declared candidates and actual public results. It returns one candidate label or an abstention symbol. A selected label compiles into exactly that entry’s tool command, which executes once. The selector cannot invent commands or revise arguments. Empty banks, unparsed results, exceeded bank limits and abstention take the original slow path. Following each fast action, its new result determines the next eligible entries.

The selector uses the same DeepSeek backbone as the slow actor, disables reasoning for the selection request, and generates one control token with model-reported log probabilities. Candidate membership and tool arguments are checked before execution. Benchmark tests evaluate the typed selection interface. The CoT-only control uses identical instructions and authors the same bank format with fast selection disabled.

The fast request retains public constraints, candidate IDs, complete arguments and the observations needed for their guards. It omits the full tool catalog, skill library, trajectory and slow rationale; unsupported states defer before selection. Candidate construction, typed selection and context compaction retain their separate mechanism identities and complete costs. Historical adapter settings and interface probes remain in the external reproduction artifacts.

Complete-task cost includes the slow actor’s bank authorship, every fast input and control token, failures and slow fallbacks. Cached inputs remain counted. The single-encoding policy supplies each decoded tool result once to the fast selector and binds it to the original receipt hash; the full original history remains available to slow reasoning. Noncanonical or unsupported observations defer to CoT. Section 5.3 distinguishes the implemented mechanism, its TRAIN comparison and final held-out evidence.

The historical ALFWorld adapter has a different candidate producer: handwritten state tracking records pickup, transformations and placement, then selects the first tool action in the highest-priority supported group. It uses neither model selection nor probability scores. Table 8 and Figure 4 disable that controller and compare instructions under a common actor. These measurements are retained as instruction and historical-controller evidence.

C.5 Terminal adapter: answer acceptance

An answer adapter supplies a terminal candidate to the same controller. The recorded text-QA adapter first generates a draft from the complete source context and retrieved original rule sentences, with fixed output budget LdraftL_{\mathrm{draft}}. Its support predicate checks the answer format, source location, and explicit answer type. Acceptance returns the draft unchanged. Rejection calls the original actor with the full selected instructions. An input-only applicability check bypasses draft generation for explicit negative/comparison questions and multiple blanks.

The draft is a model call, and fallback is a second model call. The original QA baseline has no separate verifier call to remove. This adapter can change request and response lengths while adding calls on rejected drafts; the action adapter instead avoids supported reasoning calls. Both are measured with complete-task accounting. Stored DELETE/MODIFY routing, source-rule retrieval, and the independently evaluated offline rule-development loop are specified in Appendix B.

Appendix D Execution contract, algorithm and evidence attribution

HarnessMM replaces repeated reasoning calls with stored actions through a contract between a slow author, a persistent executor and the existing native harness boundary. A directed action graph alone is a standard executable planning representation. Here each admitted continuation has immutable arguments, public feedback can only change its readiness, and the native request ledger records omission of a specified reasoning callback. These restrictions make reuse inspectable. They do not imply that every authored action is correct or every graph lowers cost.

D.1 State and execution algorithm

A graph instance contains an authored root action, a finite acyclic set of future nodes, literal native arguments, dependencies and public guards. Runtime state contains the completed native receipts, the remaining graph nodes and the public episode history. Graph content and runtime state are different objects: completing a predecessor changes the latter without rewriting the authored action.

  1. 1.

    At a native decision boundary, register the parent callback and ingest the preceding public tool receipt. Validate its association with the action that produced it.

  2. 2.

    Construct the eligible set from unresolved nodes whose dependencies are complete, public guards pass and arguments meet the adapter’s closure checks.

  3. 3.

    If exactly one node is eligible, use the declared deterministic route. If several are eligible, the configured typed selector chooses a candidate ID or abstains. Charge any model-based selector input and output.

  4. 4.

    On admission, execute the selected literal arguments through the original native interface. Record the result and compare it with the authored node. Emit an omission certificate only after checking execution and absence of the registered slow request. Mark the node completed and retain the unresolved remainder of the graph.

  5. 5.

    On rejection, an empty set or abstention, invoke the original slow actor with its public task context. Record the author request and any fallback. A newly authored graph replaces the unresolved remainder; already executed receipts remain in the episode history.

  6. 6.

    Continue under the common benchmark limits. A terminal answer uses the same commitment point and stops. The native scorer evaluates the complete task; the request ledger charges every paid call.

This algorithm describes the full mechanism. The coding adapter uses literal terminal commands and observed tool results. Instruction-only and answer-acceptance studies use different candidate producers, stated in Appendix C; they cannot be treated as independent demonstrations of persistent coding graphs.

D.2 Closure, guards and structural invariants

Literal closure and semantic closure.

Literal closure is a syntactic restriction: all executable arguments have concrete values, with no placeholder to bind from unseen feedback. It is checked by the action schema and candidate-membership audit. Semantic closure is stronger: prior reasoning has determined the action’s meaning and its future applicability is captured by the declared guard. A concrete command can still be semantically wrong. General semantic closure is therefore not established merely by parsing literal arguments.

For a fixed authored decision dd and public state ss, let valid⁡(d,s)\operatorname{valid}(d,s) mean that the action has its intended task meaning at that state. Interpreting guard acceptance as semantic permission additionally assumes

eligible⁡(d,s)=1⟹valid⁡(d,s).\operatorname{eligible}(d,s)=1\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{valid}(d,s). (12)

This implication depends on the adapter and the authored guard. The implementation enforces the left-hand checks; complete native task evaluation measures their quality consequences. There is no statewise correctness guarantee for arbitrary tools or tasks.

Argument immutability.

Assume the configured adapter uses the validated graph and native interface, the graph objects are not modified after authoring, and the recorded receipts are faithful. A reused node executes the literal arguments authored for that node. The typed selector returns only a node ID; it has no argument-generation interface. Native dispatch reads the selected stored arguments, and certificate verification compares those values with the tool receipt. This establishes an execution invariant under the stated assumptions, independently of task success.

Dependency-respecting execution.

Initially, no future node is completed. At each transition, eligibility admits only a node whose predecessor receipts are in the completion map. A completed node is removed from the unresolved set. Induction over transitions therefore gives predecessor-respecting execution with at most one dispatch per node instance. The initial acyclicity check prevents a future node from requiring its own completion. A later author call can create an identical graph, but it is a separate paid authoring event.

Omission evidence.

A valid certificate binds the authored graph instance, selected node, exact native arguments, predecessor receipt, tool receipt and registered callback. The physical request ledger independently establishes absence of the specified slow request at that boundary. This is a structural observation about the executed route. It does not establish an identical counterfactual trajectory, an absent call’s token quantity, or a task-quality improvement. Comparisons on the same full task sets measure these effects.

D.3 Break-even analysis without counterfactual token attribution

Let AA denote additional author and selector actor tokens and FF additional fallback tokens. If KK eliminated callbacks would have costs c1,…,cKc_{1},\ldots,c_{K}, a same-trajectory token calculation gives net saving only when ∑jcj>A+F\sum_{j}c_{j}>A+F. Under the simplifying assumption of a common callback cost c>0c>0, the condition is K>(A+F)/cK>(A+F)/c. This relation describes the dependence on reuse coverage; it is not a prediction of measured saving, because the omitted calls are not executed and the substituted trajectory can differ.

The reported estimator is instead the difference in total tokens across all episodes for each method. Every arm uses the same independent task membership and execution contract, and each arm’s numerator includes its actual author, selector, slow, finalization and paid unsuccessful calls. Shared authoring is assigned once to its declared population. Cached provider input remains counted under the token protocol. CPU guards and native tools affect time and behavior, but their work cannot be added to a token total without an independently defined resource conversion.

D.4 Novelty and closest mechanisms

ReWOO separates planning from tool observations and supports dependency-bound evidence variables [43]; LLMCompiler plans and dispatches tool dependencies for parallel execution [19]. Voyager develops a library of executable skills reused across tasks [40]. ActionEngine constructs application-level state-machine memory, compiles task programs and repairs execution reactively [52]. HarnessMM shares executable planning and reuse with these approaches. Its narrower contract stores episode-specific literal actions, lets public receipts activate them without argument synthesis, and binds observed native execution to a removed harness callback. We do not compare these planning systems experimentally, so the present evidence establishes the contract and benefits against the declared native harnesses rather than superiority over all executable planners.

D.5 Core method and companion configuration map

The core execution transformation has three operations: author literal future actions, retain and activate them using public feedback, and dispatch an eligible action while omitting its registered callback. Its controller selects an action route. A surrounding configuration fixes the author prompt, context serializer, native adapter and finalization rules before the run. Those settings determine what the controller receives; the controller does not search over them during an episode.

The reported studies use the following configurations. A row with no persistent execution is a companion-policy study, even when its selected policy carries the HarnessMM display label. The original run identities and exact configuration files remain in the external reproduction bundle.

Study Fixed surrounding intervention Role of executable reuse
Coding harness pairs Literal-bank author prompt, compact public context and harness-specific finalization EDG/GDR/CCS enabled; complete pair measures the integrated configuration
MBPP mechanism ablation Common author prompt, schema, public context, native tools and limits Change graph execution, persistence or callback retention to test the core mechanism
ALFWorld Selected task-family and general instructions under a common actor Instruction-only comparison; local controller disabled
SearchQA Frozen input-only profile routing, retrieved rule sentences, full-source draft and paid fallback Terminal answer acceptance; no persistent multi-action graph
LiveMath Answer-first prompt, disabled thinking and reduced output cap One call per question; no callback substitution
AIME Frozen compiled decision policy, shared authorship and domain fallback Measures the selected policy; execution or abstention follows its fixed applicability rules
Terminal-Bench overview Archived AutoSaddler-derived instruction policy Instruction-policy snapshot; no certified EDG execution claim
GAIA2 Frozen literal-bank authoring and public-context handling Integrated native execution; verified fast actions and complete costs reported together

This map also separates cost mechanisms. Shorter prompts or context change the tokens in a remaining call; EDG execution changes whether a registered call occurs. The MBPP ablations keep instruction, context and finalization settings fixed while varying graph reuse and callback execution. No experiment in this paper trains a general policy that dynamically composes these optimization techniques.

The token-efficiency prompt and objective apply to every comparison arm, including No Skill, SkillOpt, AutoSaddler, the native industrial harnesses and HarnessMM. No Skill retains the token-efficiency instruction while omitting the added skill policy. Every arm is instructed to reduce complete-task input-plus-output token consumption while preserving task performance. Method-specific mechanisms and native execution limits follow the configurations above.

D.6 Which experiment supports which claim?

Evidence Measured intervention Supported interpretation
HumanEval and MBPP harness pairs Selected HarnessMM configuration versus its original harness Complete task quality and actor cost for that implementation
MBPP single-use graphs Limit each graph to one reused action Effect of retaining graphs across tool calls
MBPP retained callbacks Invoke the registered slow callback while retaining graph execution Effect of callback removal with tasks and execution settings fixed
Native execution certificates Match authored actions, public receipts and absent requests Structural execution and callback omission
ALFWorld instruction comparison Change instructions under a common actor Effect of selected instruction content, not EDG substitution
SearchQA and AIME studies Benchmark-specific selected policies and cost components Their declared quality–cost trade-offs, with actual phases retained

The integrated coding results also change context management and finalization. Total call-count reduction can therefore exceed certificate counts; these quantities are not expected to agree. The MBPP ablation supplies a more direct intervention test but does not isolate the intrinsic value of recording a certificate from the value of exclusive routing. Certificates are a measurement mechanism, and their logging overhead is included where it makes model calls.

D.7 Historical development evidence

Historical MBPP comparisons on 85 training tasks provide development mechanism evidence: Codex improves from 91.76% to 94.12% at 67.21 versus 59.78 Tokens/task (k); DeepSeek Harness improves from 85.88% to 94.12% at 15.46 Tokens/task (k) versus 11.91 Tokens/task (k). The DeepSeek candidate records 153 certified substitutions and 62 public-guard confirmations. Across 32 GAIA2 development scenarios, Codex improves from 37.50% to 40.62% at 907.06 versus 825.99 Tokens/task (k), and DeepSeek Harness improves from 40.62% to 46.88% at 891.75 Tokens/task (k) versus 750.53 Tokens/task (k). Figure 3 preserves the earlier four panels and adds two separate MiMo panels; the appendix records their evidence phases.

The w/o skills condition averages 41.69% at 34.10 Tokens/task (k); mismatched-family and neutral instructions of equal token length reach 48.34% at 43.28 Tokens/task (k) and 41.37% at 43.26 Tokens/task (k). HarnessMM gains 24.00 points over the w/o skills condition while using 7.81% fewer tokens, and gains 24.33 points over neutral text with 27.33% fewer tokens. Every action uses the common actor and the same 50-step cap. Whiskers show the observed seed range; task identities are not independent across repetitions. Appendix I.3 preserves all per-seed counts, paired intervals and costs, including the two original seed-9401 reference conditions reused exactly once. These instruction ablations measure content effects under a common actor.

D.8 Complete quality–cost trade-offs

Across 18 Terminal-Bench development tasks, Codex success falls from 77.78% to 55.56% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 3426.78 to 1089.95; DeepSeek Harness falls from 55.56% to 50.00% at 1586.15 versus 1144.32 Tokens/task (k).

A complete CoT/Jev TEST comparison executes verified fast actions in 94.44% of episodes, yet costs 127.07% more than the original harness and loses 7.29 success points. It saves only 1.04% against CoT-only, with input tokens accounting for 98.53% of the actor ledger. The coding control on 18 training tasks likewise records 10, 12 and 13 successes for the original harness, CoT-only and CoT/Jev, while CoT/Jev costs 30.37% more than the original harness and 3.74% more than CoT-only. Appendix H preserves the complete controls and their costs.

D.9 Reproducibility and use scope

The executable adapter requires a declared native boundary, literal action serialization, public-state guards, callback registration and complete request logging. External reproduction artifacts retain frozen task memberships, model and software identities, integer costs, selection configuration and complete native outcomes. Shared optimizers use training evidence; validation selects among frozen candidates, and selected held-out configurations remain unchanged. Benchmarks with historical development populations retain their actual phase rather than being relabeled as final tests.

The controller preserves the parent’s tool permissions and action space. It does not enlarge those permissions or establish a general safety guarantee. Incorrect authorship, incomplete guards and changed tool semantics can affect task quality even when the structural certificate is valid. These cases are handled by the native evaluator and the declared quality constraint, not by treating omission evidence as correctness evidence.

Appendix E Second ablation: GDR and CCS

We evaluate four conditions on the complete MBPP-sanitized release using a custom 85/85/257 training/validation/test partition, seed 20261005. DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1 uses the shared backbone. All arms share the author prompt and schema, public context, native buffered parser, tools, decoding settings, one attempt per task, two workers per arm, and 300-second actor/30-second verifier limits. The tool working directory is /app; the latest actual public-check call and result remain in public context. Authored public assertions must match the original problem line by line. Rejected banks retain their authoring cost and return to paid native slow reasoning. Disabled-thinking requests use the same transport mapping across arms; task reasoning and output limits remain fixed.

TRAIN supplies method revisions. The sole TRAIN-qualified candidate is frozen before validation; the predeclared aggregate capability criterion selects it before TEST. Validation trajectories and test outcomes supply no method revisions. The final comparison contains all 1,028 task-arm executions. Tokens/task (k) include physical input and output from authorship, selectors, control, native recovery and unsuccessful executions, divided by 257 and 1,000.

Full HarnessMM combines GDR and CCS: GDR retains the executable graph across tool transitions; CCS replaces slow callbacks with authored actions and certifies their removal. W/o GDR (single-use EDG) discards the graph after its first certified execution, preserving its author and full authoring cost. W/o CCS (callbacks retained) retains a paid slow callback to regenerate each selected tool action. This intervention isolates callback substitution, not the independent benefit of certification. Without EDG execution preserves the author and its cost while disabling executable graph use.

Full HarnessMM performs 407 certified bypasses; 201 graphs are reused twice. W/o GDR performs 212 bypasses and discards 212 graphs. The retained-callback condition performs 257 paid regenerations and zero certified bypasses; disabling EDG produces zero bypasses. Full HarnessMM solves two more tasks than W/o GDR while reducing measured complete cost by 26.91%. Compared with retained callbacks it solves one more task at 19.52% lower cost. Relative to disabled EDG, its 18.62% cost saving accompanies four fewer correct tasks.

The reuse cost interval excludes zero; all three correctness intervals include zero. Callback and EDG cost intervals include zero. One execution per task quantifies task variation, rather than between-run variation.

E.1 Earlier execution ablation

Figure 4 complements the ALFWorld instruction ablation with execution interventions on MBPP-sanitized [2]. Instructions, authoring format, public guards and dependency checks are fixed across the HarnessMM conditions.

E.1.1 Benchmark and evaluation settings

We use the complete 427-task MBPP-sanitized release with a custom 85/85/257 training/validation/test partition, seed 20261005. Deterministic rounding implements the required 20/20/60 ratio; task membership is disjoint and common to all arms. The parent is DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1 with the shared backbone. All conditions share the public task interface, native tools, decoding settings, two workers per arm, one execution per task and 300-second actor/30-second verifier deadlines. Correctness evaluates every released assertion. Reference implementations are absent from the actor workspace.

Training supplies the structured author and frozen intervention definitions. The complete training comparison uses 85 tasks; disjoint validation selects frozen candidates without returning trajectories or failures to optimization. The historical evaluation uses the complete 257-task test population for every arm. Test outcomes supply no selection or revisions; the external archive retains every arm and execution.

E.1.2 Execution interventions

The original harness uses ordinary slow reasoning without EDG authoring or fast routing. Full HarnessMM combines the structured EDG, public eligibility checks and certified callback bypass. W/o GDR (the single-use GDR control) preserves the author and graph capacity, but discards unused nodes after its first certified execution. Unused authored nodes still incur cost.

The W/o CCS condition keeps fast selection but asks the same slow actor to regenerate exactly one tool action before execution. Changed arguments invalidate dependent nodes; invalid regeneration returns control to slow reasoning. A retained callback receives no substitution certificate. Graph authorship, selector input and control, regeneration, fallbacks and unsuccessful executions all contribute to Tokens/task (k), normalized by the full 257-task population. Development and selection costs remain separate from final execution.

E.1.3 Complete results and paired uncertainty

Full HarnessMM reduces cost by 76.19% relative to the original harness and increases observed correctness by 2.72 percentage points. The paired 95% interval for the correctness difference is [−1.95,7.39][-1.95,7.39] points; it does not establish a significant accuracy gain. Full HarnessMM makes 459 certified substitutions, with at least two bypasses in 228 authored graphs. W/o GDR (the single-use GDR control) makes 237 substitutions and discards 237 graphs after one use. Recorded slow calls per task rise from 4.49 for full HarnessMM to 5.42 for the single-use GDR control and 6.41 when callbacks are retained. The retained-callback condition records 281 callbacks and 280 regenerated actions, with zero certified bypasses.

The additional EDG reuse is active, but the single-use GDR control has slightly higher correctness and lower aggregate cost in this comparison. Retaining slow callbacks increases measured cost by 10.34% and correctness by 1.56 points; the paired intervals include equal cost and correctness. One execution per task measures task-level variation rather than run-to-run variability.

F.2 Additional study scope

Local decisions require a task-specific public-state adapter and support rules. The interactive measurements use textual ALFWorld observations; they do not establish visual-agent improvement. The ALFWorld instruction comparison transfers archived optimized policies without rerunning their optimizers. The custom test uses one seed and shares some floorplans across partitions. The ALFWorld comparisons and text-QA studies use previously exposed public data. GQA grounding and generic instructions of equal token length both score 65% in the small visual pilot. The separate rule-development pilot accepts no updates.

F.3 TRAIN substitution attribution

The attribution audit uses complete training set (32 tasks) comparisons only. Cached inputs, failed episodes, fast requests and slow fallback remain charged. The shared author is reused physically and charged once to each bank arm. No validation or TEST trajectory supplies these diagnoses.

In v20, 281 fast attempts produce 249 locally bypassed slow callbacks; 32 abstentions incur 212.17 slow-fallback Tokens/task (k). Fast requests cost 50.46 Tokens/task (k), including 18.91 input Tokens/task (k). Their removal alone would save only 1.18% of the complete bank-arm cost. The arm still makes 618 slow calls against 502 baseline attempts. It uses 79.68% more tokens and loses 6.25 success points despite fast actions in 93.75% of episodes.

The passive benchmark audit verifies 227 local substitutions in 31 episodes; 22 compiled actions in one failed SDK episode remain unresolved. Bank-bearing slow requests jointly perform reasoning and candidate construction, so their full request cost is not an isolated authoring cost.

The v22 revision reduces slow calls from 15.69 to 12.63 per episode and saves 15.55% at 43.75% versus 40.62% baseline success. Renewing banks at every slow step in v23 raises cost by 20.20% and loses one success. The full training attribution and all historical interface probes remain in the external evidence and reproduction artifacts.

F.4 Additional related-work and adapter context

Finally, uncertainty in model evaluation arises at multiple levels: task sampling, prompt choice, random seeds, execution order, and numerical/runtime behavior [31, 48, 10]. Repeating one task characterizes its execution distribution, with the task remaining the independent sampling unit. We use paired source-group estimates, retain all comparison endpoints, and separate exploratory inspection from frozen comparisons [7, 32, 6]. Crossed and nested dependence must be treated explicitly rather than pooling all response cells as independent samples [29]. Efficient serving mechanisms such as PagedAttention address execution resources [20]; repeated-request controls characterize variability under the chosen runtime.

The closest evaluation alternatives already address substantial parts of our question. FormatSpread quantifies spurious prompt-format sensitivity [35]; ProSA and POSIX examine prompt sensitivity at finer granularity [54, 3]; PromptEval estimates performance distributions over prompts efficiently [31]. PARC analyzes language/image transformations in vision-language models, with certainty derived from conformal answer scores rather than repeated execution [34]. Our comparisons combine instruction-content controls with repeated execution and image interventions. They examine how these sources of variation affect the interpretation of a quality–cost comparison.

Vision-language systems combine image representations with instruction following, and visual-programming approaches expose intermediate operations that can be inspected or recombined [22, 37]. These approaches motivate treating instructions as controls over visual decisions. Balanced and compositional benchmarks, contrastive examples, and image interventions examine complementary aspects of this problem [11, 14, 18, 26]. Our true-image and shuffled-image conditions provide a within-sample diagnostic of image dependence. The same commit-or-defer interface accepts terminal answers. A text-QA adapter obtains an actor-generated draft, checks its source, type, and format, and either returns it or calls the original answering procedure. The draft and fallback are both charged. The action adapter can avoid reasoning calls, whereas the answer adapter changes request and response lengths. Both preserve the benchmark task interface, and complete-task accounting covers every model call along either path.

Appendix G Benchmark results

G.1 Fresh ALFWorld instruction comparison and skill removal

Figures 2(a) and 4 use the same 2,133 test identities and seed 9401. The complete 3,553-task official TRAIN pool is partitioned into 710 training, 710 validation and 2,133 test tasks. Goal/scene trial variants stay together; the 240 known predecessor development tasks remain in training. This is a custom partition of previously exposed public data, with some floorplans shared across splits. The selected instructions and common actor are frozen before fresh execution. Training supplies six task-family operability checks per condition. All 710 validation tasks per condition must pass benchmark replay and cost verification before the complete test phase opens. No validation or test outcome selects or changes a policy.

All four displayed conditions share Qwen3.5-9B, temperature zero, disabled thinking, two-step history, a 2,048-token response cap and the benchmark 50-step limit. The instruction comparison deploys archived optimized artifacts without rerunning SkillOpt or AutoSaddler optimization. The skill-removal pair compares the frozen HarnessMM instructions with empty task-family instruction strings, producing the same No Skill condition as Figure 2(a). Both use the original actor for every action. All unsuccessful episodes remain in both denominators.

Adding the frozen task-family skills gives 603 paired gains and 93 losses, a net 23.91-point difference (pointwise 95% floorplan-cluster interval [19.15, 28.34]). It reduces complete-task model tokens by 8.60%. This is a secondary descriptive comparison selected for the current ablation presentation after execution; it does not replace the archived campaign’s predeclared primary contrast.

All 8,532 displayed test executions pass independent environment trajectory replay and complete provider accounting, following 2,840 validation executions and 24 training operability checks for these four policies. Their test execution costs 51.70 Tokens/task (k). The original acquisition also contains a retired handwritten-controller condition, which is excluded from the current comparison and ablation. All of its records and costs remain preserved. Complete research acquisition costs, including retired conditions and historical optimization, remain separate in the external evidence. Cumulative token termination is disabled.

The source bundle’s evidence/alfworld_fresh226_panel.json binds the complete global audit, all seven benchmark-audited test receipts, frozen policies, exact split membership and figure reproduction code. The earlier 134-task and development set (60 tasks) measurements remain archived and do not populate either current ALFWorld figure.

G.2 Full SearchQA comparison

The historical full comparison uses all 16,980 public MRQA SearchQA development questions and the official EM/F1 scorer [8]. All seven conditions in Table 10 use fresh executions with the ALFWorld Qwen3.5-9B checkpoint, BF16, temperature zero, disabled thinking, seed 20260918, a 32,768-token context and a 512-token output cap per call. SkillOpt and AutoSaddler deploy archived optimized instructions. The refined controller removes only the question-echo rejection from the preceding recovery condition.

HarnessMM adds 18 exact matches to original HarnessMM while saving 22.75% of tokens, but remains more expensive than No Skill and AutoSaddler. The complete study contains 118,860 outcomes, 119,768 actor calls and 2.27 Tokens/task (k), with no unknown usage. In the separate preceding six-condition run, tracing 500 actual post-draft recoveries gives 19 corrections and one regression. All corrections follow source-location rejection; 105 echo-triggered recoveries add 0.67 Tokens/task (k), averaged over the 500 audited recoveries without an EM gain. Against a freshly generated no-recovery control, that preceding recovery arm adds 12 exact matches at 4.04% higher cost. The distinction separates recovery within a recorded draft from variability between independently generated drafts. Its complete records remain in generated/searchqa_full_9b_appendix.tex.

G.3 Cross-dataset QA transfer

The same full-source recovery adapter is evaluated with frozen Qwen3.8-27B on four complete MRQA development archives (Table 11). BF16, temperature zero, disabled thinking, seed 20260918 and the 512-token per-call output cap are common to all conditions. HotpotQA’s checksum-verified archive contains all 5,901 questions. TriviaQA uses the complete web archive.

Recovery adds 0.05–0.15 EM points over the no-recovery draft at higher cost. Relative to original HarnessMM, SearchQA gains 14 exact matches but loses 0.004 F1 points, hidden by rounding in the table; the other three datasets improve both metrics. HarnessMM exceeds all three external prompt controls in EM and F1, while No Skill and AutoSaddler use fewer tokens. These are single-seed point estimates.
