G.5 Success-first coding search

The instruction module improves the original coding harness’s development outcomes while reducing complete-task token use (Table 13). The study uses all 18 TRAIN tasks in the frozen 18/18/53 Terminal-Bench 2.0 partition [12], Codex 0.142.5 [28] and DeepSeek-flash. The original task, common completion brief, original tools, task limits and binary verifier are identical across conditions. The built-in-compaction control uses Codex’s own 65,536-token trigger without reducing the model’s context capacity.

Both proposed instructions solve 14 tasks. The second retains that training success count while reducing actor tokens from 2202.94 to 1455.83 Tokens/task (k). It requires persisting every requested artifact, checking exact paths and fields, extending working interfaces, and recovering from observed setup errors before optional exploration. Against the corrected original harness, it gains four successes and uses 39.68% fewer actor tokens; against built-in compaction, it gains two successes and uses 29.25% fewer. Descriptive paired-task bootstrap intervals for the training score differences are [5.56,44.44][5.56,44.44] and [−11.11,33.33][-11.11,33.33] percentage points, respectively (10,000 resamples, seed 20260928). The selected instruction is frozen for a separate four-arm study on 18 validation and 53 TEST tasks, with five executions per TEST task.

Complete development acquisition costs are retained separately from validation and deployment. The external evidence preserves exact costs, benchmark verdicts, instructions and paired task results.

We then adapt AutoSOTA’s objective-and-reflection workflow [39] to built-in context management. This is a workflow adaptation, with the official CLI unused. The search holds the instruction and original execution settings fixed, requires at least the instruction’s 14 successes, and minimizes complete-task input-plus-output tokens. Its first round tests a 32,768-token compaction trigger; the frozen feedback rule chooses a shorter trigger only if quality is preserved and tokens fall, and a longer trigger otherwise. The 40% parent-relative saving target does not end the search early.

The complete 32Ki round uses 1068.67 actor Tokens/task (k): 55.72% fewer tokens than the original harness and 26.59% fewer than the instruction module. It solves 61.11% of tasks and loses three of the instruction’s successes, with no gains over that instruction. The paired training-score difference is −16.67-16.67 percentage points (descriptive 95% task-bootstrap interval [−33.33,0.00][-33.33,0.00]). The quality guard rejects this candidate and evaluates the frozen 98,304-token successor. That round also solves 61.11% of tasks, with one gain and four losses relative to the instruction. Its paired training-score difference is −16.67-16.67 percentage points (descriptive 95% task-bootstrap interval [−38.89,5.56][-38.89,5.56]). It uses 1176.39 actor Tokens/task (k), 51.26% fewer than the original harness and 19.20% fewer than the instruction, but 10.08% more than the 32Ki round. Both candidates therefore fail the 77.78% quality requirement and remain ineligible for protected validation. The two completed rounds add 2245.06 Tokens/task (k) to development expenditure. Table 13 retains both complete trade-offs. The original harness and selected instruction remain in this TRAIN table. Figure 3 reserves coding cells for complete, audited held-out comparisons.

Appendix H Industrial-harness RSI comparison

Codex 0.142.5 uses the Responses API; DeepSeek Harness dsh-v0.2.0-rc.1 uses the Messages API. Both use DeepSeek-flash, byte-preserving metering, the ARE 1.1.0 scorer and the custom GAIA2-mini 32/32/96 split (seed 20260928). Each descendant is paired with its own industrial seed.

Each search makes two sparse-instruction proposals on all 32 training scenarios. The second receives the first candidate’s training feedback. A grouped cross-fitted router admits only positive supported advantage; protected validation selects among admitted candidates and the seed. Codex applies residual instructions through task-local AGENTS.md; DeepSeek uses an additive system-prompt section. Original execution loops, tools, model and task limits stay fixed. Policy, adapter, scorer and source hashes freeze before testing; validation failures and test outcomes never enter the proposer.

Both searches reject their two candidates and retain the seed. The complete tests compare independent executions of each unchanged harness: Codex records 10.42% versus 9.03% success; DeepSeek records 8.68% versus 7.64%. The execution component alone is 4.82 Tokens/task (k); it remains above No Skill’s 4.59 before adding authorship. Thus the full comparison measures a small output reduction alongside higher input and shared cost.

Compiled AIME continuation.

The frozen six-card program bank preserves 100.00% TRAIN correctness at 4.68 Tokens/task (k): five model-based one-token judges consume 0.89 Tokens/task (k) and three original-harness fallbacks contribute 3.79 Tokens/task (k), normalized over all six tasks. The two offline CoT author calls consume 21.98 Tokens/task (k) separately. The complete validation comparison preserves its benchmark quality floor but misses the earlier cost targets. Under the October 6 all-outcomes reporting instruction, the same bank proceeds to the fixed test set (18 tasks) without further method updates. Training improvements and the complete validation result retain their actual phases; no TEST result is used for selection or revision.

Exact-union packing merges overlapping source windows without changing characters or order, then refills the budget using the frozen 256-question TRAIN ranker and target-role contract. Union 704 leads the family at 76.23% EM, saving 61.82% of incumbent tokens and 28.58% against No Skill. It recovers 30 of 58 net lost answers, leaving a 0.825-point EM gap. A 1,000-resample question/context-group bootstrap gives an EM-difference interval of [−1.89,+0.21][-1.89,+0.21] points and token-ratio interval [0.374,0.389][0.374,0.389] against the incumbent. These TRAIN intervals do not establish noninferiority; the exact-union family did not advance to validation or TEST. None of 25 earlier five-fold/penalty recovery fits recovers all 2,616 answers within 0.98 Tokens/task (k). Those estimates reuse recorded outcomes and costs without new actor calls.

On AIME, eliminate-then-evaluate preserves 100.00% accuracy at 18.63% higher cost; the other two candidates lose one answer and cost more than No Skill. The answer-aware seven-policy oracle needs 5.52 Tokens/task (k) versus the 5.30 Tokens/task (k) target.

An earlier GAIA2 development comparison uses 32 training scenarios with three benchmark executions each. No Skill solves 30.21% at 687.35 Tokens/task (k); the frozen official AutoSaddler selection solves 38.54% at 809.18 Tokens/task (k). Their respective native judge costs are 3.68 and 3.44 Tokens/task (k), and optimizer expenditure remains separate from execution.

The selected GAIA2 incumbent improves validation and saves 11.18% of actor tokens. The respective 2.72 and 3.94 judge Tokens/task (k) give 11.00% combined saving. Token-wire v3 loses quality and increases actor cost by 37.08%, with 2.15 separate judge Tokens/task (k) and no unknown usage or context rejections. Lazy schemas lose quality at 10.82% higher actor cost. Exact ledger references preserve all 24 paired outcomes with 17.02% fewer actor tokens. References to unchanged tool actions/observations replace duplicated receipts; task and tool contracts remain intact. Parent/candidate use 472/474 paid actor calls and 124,328/120,968 judge tokens.

On all 32 TRAIN scenarios (Table 19), official SoL-Pi [23] saves 71.42–71.45% of Pi’s actor tokens with 33.33% versus 20.83% success. It gains five successes over No Harness at 2.928–2.930 times the cost. Historical HarnessMM exact references reach 43.75%, saving 36.07% against their parent, 22.15% against No Harness and 73.41–73.43% against this SoL-Pi adapter. This is separate from the CoT/Jev core: its earlier candidate scores 37.50% versus 50.00%, saves 5.29%, and defers all 276 typed decisions. The 50% No Harness saving target remains unmet.

The prospective progress-recovery parent also fails its success-first TRAIN gate. An explicit unmet-constraint checklist and tool-error recovery solves 0.00% of scenarios, compared with 3.13% for the original harness, while using 28.41% more actor tokens. The 64 executions account for 604.83 actor Tokens/task (k) exactly once. Input/output usage is complete; dollar cost and cache-write usage remain unknown. Validation and TEST stay sealed, so this result rejects the revision without informing selection on either protected split.

The complete 32-scenario validation diagnostic rejects both uses of the TRAIN-derived candidate. Direct application loses one success and uses 14.71% more actor tokens than the original harness. Frozen routing applies the candidate once, preserves 6.25% success, and uses 3.37% more tokens. The 96 executions use 745.50 measured actor Tokens/task (k) with no missing token records. These validation outcomes select neither a method revision nor a paper claim, and TEST remains sealed.

The DeepSeek validation study solves 3.13% of scenarios under every mode. Direct application uses 25.47% fewer actor tokens on this observed population, while frozen routing applies no residual and saves 6.76%. The 96 executions use 666.88 measured actor Tokens/task (k) with complete, unique request and tool-receipt accounting. One repetition with one success per mode does not establish a capability improvement or population-level noninferiority; TEST remains sealed and dollar costs are unknown.

Exact acquisition and inherited development expenditure are retained separately in the external evidence. Benchmark outcome and complete execution-usage audits accompany the frozen policies.

I.2 Latest complete TRAIN follow-ups

Figure 2’s lower strip reports complete development cohorts. SearchQA risk-220 combines the TRAIN-fitted answer-support ranker, greedy source packing and a frozen recovery policy. On all 3,395 TRAIN questions it records 77.53% EM at 0.97 Tokens/task (k), versus the incumbent’s 77.05% at 2.29 Tokens/task (k): 57.65% fewer tokens and a +0.471-point observed EM difference. The paired 95% interval is [−0.471,1.443][-0.471,1.443] points (1,000 question/context-group resamples). The complete official-control comparison and subsequent validation rejection appear in Table 21. The earlier exact-union family remains in Table 17.

AIME readout v4 preserves 100.00% accuracy but uses 15.54 Tokens/task (k); the unchanged 5.30 Tokens/task (k) target is 80% of the cheapest named control. Both model-based one-token readouts reject their checkpoint; all six questions use incumbent fallback. The independent audit reconstructs all 30 outcomes and 38 paid calls (8.64 Tokens/task (k) across five conditions). The cost gate rejects v4; its drafts and decisions remain charged.

The GAIA2 non-unknown rank gate executes 23 typed fast actions and solves 37.50%, matching the fresh original gate’s total success count while using 14.68% fewer actor tokens. Three successes are gained and three lost. It remains below the historical No Harness reference (50.00% at 758.40 Tokens/task (k)). The fresh original/rank gates incur 2.70 and 3.87 separate judge Tokens/task (k). These registered benchmark gates do not release the full four-method or held-out comparison.

Inherited development and instruction-search expenditure are retained separately in the external acquisition records.

AutoSOTA-guided all-method development comparison.

We adapt AutoSOTA’s baseline, diagnosis, prospective revision and independent evaluation workflow [39]; the official AutoSOTA CLI is not invoked. TRAIN fits an answer-support ranker and a risk score from public source, draft and model-reported token-probability features. Greedy source packing supplies the short answer request. The frozen risk policy assigns incumbent recovery to 220 of 3,395 questions; every initial draft and paid recovery is counted. The 6.48% recovery fraction and all model, scorer and policy hashes are fixed before validation. Validation exposes aggregate selection statistics only; no case, answer or failure trajectory enters training. Official SkillOpt and AutoSaddler receive configured pools of 2,716 optimization and 679 internal-selection questions within TRAIN. Actual distinct optimizer exposure is 3,395 questions for SkillOpt and 711 for AutoSaddler; each selected-policy TRAIN and validation evaluation covers all 3,395 questions in its split. The complete TRAIN comparison passes the all-method candidate-admission gate (Table 21).

On complete validation, risk-220 uses 0.99 Tokens/task (k) at 76.76% EM and 83.36% F1. No Skill uses 1.23 Tokens/task (k) at 69.81% EM. The token reduction is 19.08% (paired 95% interval [16.57,21.23][16.57,21.23]%), with a 6.951-point EM gain (paired 95% interval [5.685,8.277][5.685,8.277] points). Risk-220 saves 38.57% against SkillOpt while improving EM by 4.624 points, and saves 20.75% against AutoSaddler with 7.158 points higher EM. Against the HarnessMM incumbent, the saving is 56.87% with a 0.442-point EM decrease (paired 95% interval [−1.267,0.471][-1.267,0.471] points). Removing risk recovery gives 75.79% EM at 0.84 Tokens/task (k); recovery adds 0.972 EM points (paired 95% interval [0.560,1.443][0.560,1.443]). Intervals use 1,000 question/context-group resamples with seed 20260928.

The frozen release rule requires no benchmark-score regression against the strongest named control and incumbent, plus at least 20% saving against the cheapest named control. Validation misses the incumbent quality threshold and saves 19.08% against cheapest No Skill. TEST remains sealed; this comparison is an exploratory quality–cost result. All 16,980 public MRQA development questions have prior project exposure; the custom partition is not the official hidden test.

Official optimization costs are separate: the completed SkillOpt loop uses 23,542,512 actor and 8.99 proposer Tokens/task (k); AutoSaddler uses 927,732 actor and 0.11 proposer Tokens/task (k). The selected TRAIN and validation executions in the table are additional development costs. Both current p8 optimizer loops have complete usage, with zero unknown-usage calls. Inherited p7 operational attempts remain charged separately, including 2,028 SkillOpt requests with unknown usage. Administrative research-agent usage is also unknown, precluding a complete amortized-cost or break-even estimate.

Appendix J Historical diagnostics and negative results

J.1 Separating task rules from model calls

The action adapter contains a handwritten task solver. Running its unchanged public-state rules from the initial state, without skill text, actor initialization or model fallback, solves 92.39% of validation tasks versus 92.82% for rules plus actor. The three gains and zero losses give a 0.42-point difference at 1.08 additional Tokens/task (k). Fixed rules account for most success; this contrast does not isolate learned instructions from initialization and fallback.

Independent benchmark replay also reproduces all 2,010 archived outcomes and provider-token totals for the full controller, skills-only actor and three prompt controls. The historical 100% result includes handwritten task rules and does not measure an RSI optimization gain.

J.2 Archived action-controller comparisons

The complete official134 replication uses all valid_unseen tasks, seeds 9401–9403 and a common 50-step limit. The support-first handwritten controller solves 100.00% at each seed, versus 67.16%, 67.91% and 69.40% for its skills-only actor. The stall-gated predecessor solves 97.76%, 99.25% and 97.76%; removing its progress filter gives 35.07%, 32.84% and 34.33%. Removing its skill text gives 97.76%, 97.01% and 97.76%. These interventions belong to the predecessor, separate from the instruction-only ablation in Figure 4. All ten configurations and their per-seed costs remain in generated/jev_mechanism_confirmation.tex. The 134 tasks, not the 402 repeated executions, are the independent units.

On the separate custom test set (2133, tasks) support-first execution solves 95.08% of tasks at 1.00 Tokens/task (k), versus 92.55% at 9.91 for stall gating. The paired 80 gains and 26 losses give a 2.53-point difference (95% floorplan-cluster interval [0.98,4.07][0.98,4.07]) and 89.89% token saving. Both use the same instructions, selector and 50-step cap. This compares historical controller configurations. The earlier development set (60 tasks) selection used opened tasks and unequal historical limits; it supplies no additional held-out evidence.

J.3 Recorded execution examples

The archived stall-gated traces illustrate both progress and failure. In the heating example, the controller picks up egg 3 at step 13, heats it at 15, and places it in the fridge at 17. Heating feedback updates the tracked state, excluding the otherwise legal cooling action. The episode succeeds in 18 steps with seven model calls and 8.17 Tokens/task (k) for that single episode. In the two-book example, the placement ledger distinguishes the first completed book from the remaining target; the run succeeds in 22 steps with 11 calls and 9.96 Tokens/task (k). In the heated-cup failure, supported exploration reaches the still-closed fridge at the final allowed step, 48, without finding and heating the cup. Local support does not guarantee timely task completion. These are the lexicographically first recorded success/failure examples in their categories, bound in evidence/jev_execution_examples.json; they are illustrative, not additional evaluation samples.

J.4 Compression and transfer failures

Earlier SearchQA studies use 5,000 opened training-source questions. The 9B compact-context deterministic adapter reaches 70.54 EM at 1.90 Tokens/task (k) versus 75.46 at 3.00 for fresh original HarnessMM: 36.71% fewer tokens with a 4.92-point loss. Model-selected recovery reaches 73.42 at 3.02 Tokens/task (k). The later evaluations retain full source context.

The separate studies with the same backbone also fail their quality targets. Model-based typed checks reach 72.12 EM at 4.08 Tokens/task (k) versus 73.32 at 3.00 Tokens/task (k) for original HarnessMM, falling back on 87.80% of tasks. Probability-only full/compact source selection reaches 44.16/45.06 EM. Adding 96 CoT tokens gives 29.00 versus 27.06 for its fresh zero-CoT control; restoring a short evidence sentence gives 35.10 versus 19.98 for its label-alias control. The initial evidence-generation attempt was inactive and scored 20.10. Source-rule typed recovery reaches 69.72 versus 72.08 for fresh original HarnessMM, saving only 10.50% against its 30% target. Each study retains its own model, request template, complete controls and accounting in the source bundle; none replaces the later full-source result.

Spreadsheet’s opened LOGO267 replay gives 4.12% at 48.36 Tokens/task (k) for archived No Skill, 3.00% at 51.58 Tokens/task (k) for SkillOpt, 2.25% at 47.77 Tokens/task (k) for AutoSaddler, and 3.00% at 11.78 Tokens/task (k) for HarnessMM. The last three use fresh executions; HarnessMM retains 170 repair/abstention routes and 97 No-Skill routes chosen post hoc by workbook group. Its separate seven-condition test on 200 opened tasks gives deterministic recovery 2.50%, matching original HarnessMM at 25.06% lower cost, but below No Skill and AutoSaddler at 3.50%. Its 97-task state-controller study solves 0.00% versus the parent’s 1.03% while increasing cost. The earlier Terminal-Bench subset gives HarnessMM 8.33% versus 25.00% for each baseline; the visual-web subset gives 25.00% versus 33.33% for No Skill and SkillOpt.

The AIME draft-isolation diagnostic scores 70.00% versus 80.00% for both visible-draft verification and the shared drafts. GAIA2’s feedback-consistent controller reduces repeated restorations from 64 to 3 and Tokens/task (k) from 929.89 to 838.67, but scores 83.33% versus 90.00% for its original harness evaluated on the same development tasks in a new run. The older budget-limited GAIA2 run and email-pagination activation diagnostic have incomplete outcomes across methods; neither supports a quality or cost comparison.

J.5 Instruction-content and visual diagnostics

The five-module response study evaluates all 32 masks, ten equal-length body controls and Original A/A on 256 discovery tasks and 257 held-out-stage tasks in 256 source groups. The full harness solves 84.82%; the discovery-selected normalization/answer-type mask solves 84.44% at 23.91% lower cost. No module passes the primary familywise criterion, and no average main effect or pair interaction passes the Holm-corrected secondary tests. Nineteen tasks vary in EM across masks; the outcome-selected oracle reaches 86.77% and is not a deployable selector.

The targeted replication retains those 19 tasks, two F1-only cases and 32 stable controls, with six arms in eight blocks (four serial, four 16-concurrent). Eighteen of the 19 EM effects retain their mean direction, and 17 retain a nonzero sign in every block; both F1-only effects persist. Stable controls have zero EM edge effects, while Original A/A changes EM on two variable tasks. These are conditional, outcome-selected effects; 13 of the 19 nominated modules concern normalization. All retained module bytes, ordering and answer contracts are unchanged, and generic/unrelated controls exactly match complete model input token counts.

The GQA pilot evaluates 40 balanced questions in 19 image groups, plus 88 entailment-support questions, with three repeats. True-image accuracy is 62.50% for the base and 65.00% for both grounding and generic instructions of equal token length; shuffled-image accuracy is 35.00%, 33.33% and 35.00%, respectively. Grounding and generic correctness coincide on every balanced task. Their true-minus-shuffled interaction is 1.67 points, with a descriptive image-cluster interval of [−2.44,7.69][-2.44,7.69]. Images use 448-by-448 padded renderings with 196 model image tokens. The 2,304 benchmark requests consume 0.27 Tokens/task (k); admission adds 500. Model image tokens and the unchanged publisher scorer were replayed independently [14].

Two later feasibility studies also stop before final evaluation. Text calibration evaluates 512 groups over three repeats after training on 2,048 groups; all four adaptive thresholds fail the joint gate. The least restrictive saves 4.3734% while lowering EM and F1; the quality-preserving three-short-route policy saves only 0.1483%. For the MMMU instruction library, 270 calls on 90 training questions consume 0.65 Tokens/task (k), including 0.51 input-image/task (k). Even zero output permits only 0.366% saving, below the 10% target. This is a cost-feasibility bound; task accuracy was not measured. The completed gate records remain in generated/token_efficiency_protocol.tex; unexecuted plans are omitted from the paper.
